sense: a people’s way of life: its customs, beliefs and arts

terms.gloss: a people’s ways: its customs and way of life
evidence: Nep. Paus. 3.1: nōn enim mōrēs patriōs sōlum, sed etiam cultum vestītumque mūtāvit
terms.comment: With īnstitūta and lēgēs, what we call a people’s culture. For one custom see practice (custom).

terms.gloss: a way of life, civilisation: how a people lives, dresses and eats
evidence: Caes. BG 1.1.3: ā cultū atque hūmānitāte prōvinciae longissimē absunt
Cic. de Or. 1.33: ā ferā agrestīque vītā ad hunc hūmānum cultum cīvīlemque dēdūcere
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: care directed to the refinement of life, that is style, manner of life, culture, civilisation. Morgan–Owens: cultus cīvīlis, cultus hūmānus.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.1.2: hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt
terms.comment: For one established practice see practice (custom).

evidence: Tac. Agr. 21.3: idque apud inperītōs hūmānitās vocābātur
terms.comment: Tacitus, of the Britons taking to porticoes, baths and dinner parties: the naive called it civilisation, when it was part of their slavery.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.151: nihil est agrī cultūrā melius
terms.comment: Not a people’s culture: classically the tilling of land, and by metaphor the cultivation of the mind (see culture, learning and the arts).

phrases.latin: Hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt.
phrases.english: They all differ from one another in language, customs and laws.

phrases.latin: Nōn enim mōrēs patriōs sōlum, sed etiam cultum vestītumque mūtāvit.
phrases.english: For he changed not only the ways of his own country but his whole way of life and his dress as well.
